blocks.task_summary: Show that the gradient of the normal line N to H at x=t is t^2.
method_path: Differentiate y=1/x to get dy/dx = -1/x^2
Evaluate at x=t to get gradient of tangent = -1/t^2
Take negative reciprocal to get gradient of normal = t^2
accepted_alternatives: Use parametric differentiation: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) with x=t, y=1/t, leading to same result.

evidence.basis: METHOD 1: attempts to find dy/dx (M1); dy/dx = -1/x^2; dy/dx = -1/t^2 AND m_N = 1/(1/t^2) (or equivalent) A1; so gradient of N is t^2 AG. METHOD 2: uses dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) (M1); dy/dx = -1/t^2; m_N = 1/(1/t^2) A1; so gradient of N is t^2 AG.

blocks.task_summary: Show that the equation of the normal line N is y = t^2 x + (1/t) - t^3.
method_path: Use point-slope form with point (t, 1/t) and gradient t^2
Simplify to y = t^2 x + 1/t - t^3
accepted_alternatives: Use y = t^2 x + c, substitute (t, 1/t) to find c = 1/t - t^3.
Write as t^2 x - y - t^3 + 1/t = 0.

evidence.basis: EITHER y - 1/t = t^2 (x - t) OR y = t^2 x - t^3 + 1/t A1; leading to y = t^2 x + 1/t - t^3 AG. OR 1/t = t^3 + c => c = 1/t - t^3 A1. OR t^2 x - y - t^3 + 1/t = 0 A1.

method_path: Set m = t^2 and c = 1/t - t^3
Express t = ±√m
Substitute t = √m or t = -√m into c
Simplify to obtain the two expressions

evidence.basis: m = t^2 (=> m = t^2) OR c = 1/t - t^3 OR c = 1/t (1 - t^4) (A1); t = ±√m (seen anywhere) A1; substitutes one of their t = √m OR t = -√m into c = 1/t - t^3 OR c = 1/t (1 - t^4) M1; c = ±(1/√m - m√m) A1; so either c = 1/√m - √m OR c = -1/√m + √m AG.

blocks.task_summary: Determine the set of values of m for which there exists at least one line normal to H.
method_path: Recognize that m = t^2 and t ≠ 0
Conclude m > 0

blocks.task_summary: Determine the set of values of m for which there exists exactly one line normal to H.
method_path: Identify that exactly one normal occurs when the two expressions for c are equal
Solve 1/√m - √m = -1/√m + √m to get m = 1

blocks.task_summary: Determine the set of values of m for which there exist exactly two lines normal to H.
method_path: Recognize that two normals exist when the two c expressions are distinct and real
Combine with m > 0 and m ≠ 1

evidence.basis: m ∈ ℝ^+, m ≠ 1 (or equivalent) A1A1. Note: Award A1 for 0 < m < 1 and A1 for m > 1.

method_path: Draw the hyperbola y = 1/x with asymptotes at axes

evidence.basis: a correct sketch of y = 1/x A1.

blocks.task_summary: Sketch two normal lines for an appropriate m, indicating points of normality.
method_path: Choose m > 0, m ≠ 1
Draw two parallel normal lines with non-zero y-intercepts approximately equidistant from origin
Mark points where lines are normal to H

evidence.basis: a line normal to H such that c ≠ 0 A1; a second parallel line which is normal to H such that c ≠ 0 A1. Note: For normal lines that cross the y-axis, award A1A0 if the y-axis intercepts are not approximately equidistant from O. Award a maximum A1A0 for a normal line sketched for 0 < m < 1 and a normal line sketched for m > 1.

blocks.task_summary: Show that the x-coordinates of A and B satisfy the quadratic equation x^2 - k(t^3 - 1/t)x - k^2/t^2 = 0.
method_path: Set equation of normal equal to curve F: k/x^2 = t^2 x - kt^3 + k/t
Multiply by x^2 and rearrange to form quadratic in x
Simplify to given equation

evidence.basis: k/x^2 = t^2 x - kt^3 + k/t (A1); attempts to form a quadratic equation in x (M1); eg. t^2 x^3 - kt^3 x^2 + (k/t)x^2 - k = 0 OR x^2 - k(t^3 - 1/t)x - k^2/t^2 = 0 A1. Note: Award (A0)M1A0 for attempting to verify that kt is a root of the AG (or its equivalent quadratic equation). Award (A0)M0A0 for showing that A lies on F.

blocks.task_summary: Determine the coordinates of B using sum or product of roots.
method_path: Let α = kt (x-coordinate of A), β = x-coordinate of B
Use sum of roots: α + β = k(t^3 - 1/t) or product: αβ = -k^2/t^2
Solve for β = -k/t^3
Find y-coordinate by substituting into F: y = -kt^3
accepted_alternatives: Factor the quadratic: (x - kt)(x + k/t^3) = 0, giving x = -k/t^3.
Use quadratic formula to find roots, identify the one not equal to kt.

evidence.basis: METHOD 1: recognizes that the sum of roots is k(t^3 - 1/t) (M1); kt + β = k(t^3 - 1/t) OR recognizes that the product of roots is -k^2/t^2 (M1); kt * β = -k^2/t^2; THEN β = -k/t^3 is the other root A1; y = -kt^3 A1; coordinates of B are (-k/t^3, -kt^3). METHOD 2: recognizes that (x - kt) is a factor (M1); (x - kt)(x + k/t^3) = 0 => x = -k/t^3 A1; y = -kt^3 A1. METHOD 3: attempts to use the quadratic formula (M1); x = [k(t^3 - 1/t) ± √(k^2(t^3 - 1/t)^2 + 4k^2/t^2)]/2 => x = kt, -k/t^3 A1; y = -kt^3 A1.

blocks.task_summary: Prove that angle BCA is a right angle.
method_path: Identify coordinates: A(kt, k/t), B(-k/t^3, -kt^3), C(-kt, -k/t)
Find vectors CA and CB (or slopes of CA and CB)
Show dot product CA·CB = 0 (or product of slopes = -1, or AB^2 = AC^2 + BC^2)
accepted_alternatives: Show that B lies on the perpendicular to AC at C.

evidence.basis: METHOD 1: A(kt, k/t), B(-k/t^3, -kt^3), C(-kt, -k/t) (A1); attempts to find m_AC or m_BC (M1); m_AC = 1/t^2 AND m_BC = -t^2 (or equivalent) A1; attempts to find m_AC × m_BC OR recognizes that m_AC = -1/m_BC (M1); (1/t^2)(-t^2) = -1 A1; = -1 and so [BC] ⟂ [CA] R1; hence BCA is a right angle AG. METHOD 2: A(kt, k/t), B(-k/t^3, -kt^3), C(-kt, -k/t) (A1); m_AC = 1/t^2 A1; attempts to find equation of perpendicular to [AC] at C (M1); y + k/t = -t^2 (x + kt); substitutes x = -k/t^3 (M1); y = -kt^3 A1; B lies on perpendicular to [AC] at C (B ≠ C) and so [BC] ⟂ [CA] R1; hence BCA is a right angle AG. METHOD 3: A(kt, k/t), B(-k/t^3, -kt^3), C(-kt, -k/t) OR OC = (-kt, -k/t) (A1); attempts to find CA or CB (M1); CA = (2kt, 2k/t) AND CB = (-k/t^3 + kt, -kt^3 + k/t) A1; attempts to find CA·CB (M1); CA·CB = 2kt(-k/t^3 + kt) + (2k/t)(-kt^3 + k/t) = -2k^2/t^2 + 2k^2t^2 - 2k^2t^2 + 2k^2/t^2 = 0 A1; = 0 (and since t ≠ ±1, CB ≠ 0) R1; then BCA is a right angle AG. METHOD 4: A(kt, k/t), B(-k/t^3, -kt^3), C(-kt, -k/t) (A1); attempts to find one of AB^2, AC^2 or BC^2 (M1); AB^2 = (kt + k/t^3)^2 + (k/t + kt^3)^2 A1; attempts to show AB^2 = AC^2 + BC^2 (M1); AB^2 = k^2(t^2 + 2/t^2 + 1/t^6) + k^2(1/t^2 + 2t^2 + t^6) = k^2(t^2 + 3/t^2 + 1/t^6 + t^6) AND AC^2 + BC^2 = (2kt)^2 + (2k/t)^2 + (-k/t^3 + kt)^2 + (-kt^3 + k/t)^2 = 4k^2t^2 + 4k^2/t^2 + k^2/t^6 - 2k^2/t^2 + k^2t^2 + k^2t^6 - 2k^2t^2 + k^2/t^2 = k^2(t^2 + 3/t^2 + 1/t^6 + t^6) A1; AB^2 = AC^2 + BC^2 (and so, by converse of Pythagoras) R1; BCA is a right angle AG.
